note: Teaching text, clarifying questions, inferred constraints and own examples. Inferred, not official. Examples are small generated inputs with outputs from the independent references in oracles.py.

clarifyingQuestions: Do rejected requests count toward the window?
Are timestamps guaranteed sorted?
Should the result be booleans or a count?
hints: Only allowed requests occupy the window.
Requests older than t-windowSize+1 can never matter again.
Keep allowed timestamps in a queue and drop the stale front before each decision.
invariants: the queue holds exactly the allowed timestamps inside the current window
queue length <= maxRequests
chooseWhen: Timestamps arrive in order and the window is fixed
tradeoffs: A queue costs O(maxRequests) memory; a counting array would need bounded time ranges
hack2hire:68ac41b61bf7d2097f647ef1.variantLabel: Inferred: per-request allow/reject over a sliding window

constraints: up to 20000 log records, times 0..1e9 non-decreasing
clarifyingQuestions: What does each log record contain and is the log sorted?
Does re-adding an active moderator change their rank?
Can a moderator remove themselves?
hints: Replay the log once; you only need who is active and when they most recently became a moderator.
Rank by the position of the effective ADD record.
canRemove compares two ranks after checking both users are active and distinct.
invariants: rank map contains exactly the active moderators
lower rank value = higher level
chooseWhen: The log is fixed at construction and queried many times
tradeoffs: Precomputing ranks makes every check O(1) at O(U) memory

constraints: up to 20000 log records, times 0..1e9 non-decreasing
clarifyingQuestions: What does each log record contain and is the log sorted?
Does re-adding an active moderator change their rank?
Can a moderator remove themselves?
Should the list be highest-first?
hints: Level 1 ranks already define the order.
Sort active users by rank once after replay.
Return a copy so callers cannot mutate the stored order.
invariants: stored order is ascending by rank
returned lists are fresh
chooseWhen: Lists are requested repeatedly from a fixed log
tradeoffs: Sorting once costs O(U log U); per-call sorting would repeat that work

constraints: up to 20000 log records, times 0..1e9 non-decreasing
clarifyingQuestions: What does each log record contain and is the log sorted?
Does re-adding an active moderator change their rank?
Can a moderator remove themselves?
Is a query at time t inclusive of records stamped t?
hints: A user's status only changes at their effective log records.
Store, per user, the times of effective changes and the rank after each.
Binary-search that list for the last change at or before t.
invariants: per-user change times are non-decreasing
rank after a REMOVE is recorded as inactive
chooseWhen: Many historical queries over a long log
tradeoffs: Per-user histories cost O(L) memory; full snapshots per time would cost O(L*U)

clarifyingQuestions: What does a query return for an empty cell?
Are coordinates inclusive?
Can ids be reused after removal?
hints: The newest covering rectangle wins.
The board can be huge, so store rectangles, not cells.
Scan rectangles and keep the covering one with the greatest stacking key.
invariants: stacking keys strictly increase with insertion
chooseWhen: Board area is large and rectangle count is modest
tradeoffs: O(R) queries; a 2D index would add much complexity

clarifyingQuestions: What does a query return for an empty cell?
Are coordinates inclusive?
Can ids be reused after removal?
What does removing an unknown id return?
hints: Removal only hides a rectangle.
Keep an active flag per id.
Skip inactive ids during the scan.
invariants: ids are never reused
inactive rectangles never answer queries
tradeoffs: Inactive entries still cost scan time

clarifyingQuestions: What does a query return for an empty cell?
Are coordinates inclusive?
Can ids be reused after removal?
Does bringing to front change the id?
hints: Only relative stacking matters.
Give the rectangle a fresh, larger key.
Queries already pick the largest key.
invariants: keys stay unique
tradeoffs: Keys grow without bound but stay small integers here

clarifyingQuestions: What does a query return for an empty cell?
Are coordinates inclusive?
Can ids be reused after removal?
Which operations are undoable?
Does undoing an add free the id?
hints: Every successful mutation needs an inverse.
Push (kind, id, old key) on a stack.
Pop and apply the inverse: deactivate, reactivate or restore the old key.
invariants: the history stack holds only successful mutations
undo restores the exact previous stacking order
chooseWhen: Undo depth is unbounded and mutations are cheap
tradeoffs: Inverse operations avoid full-state snapshots

clarifyingQuestions: Which operators may formulas use?
Are values doubles or integers?
Should getCell reflect later edits to referenced cells?
hints: Store the formula, not its value, so edits propagate.
A cell may be referenced many times; memoise within one evaluation.
Evaluate with an explicit stack so long reference chains do not overflow recursion.
invariants: an unset cell is 0
within one getCell every cell is evaluated once
chooseWhen: Reads are less frequent than writes
tradeoffs: Evaluation on read is O(V+E) per read; eager propagation would make writes expensive
hack2hire:69f78c6830f41dfd539fc6dc.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: live formulas without cycles

clarifyingQuestions: What should happen when a formula creates a cycle?
Is a self-reference a cycle?
Does a rejected set keep the old content?
hints: A new formula creates a cycle only if the target is reachable from what it references.
Search the current reference graph from the new references.
Reject before storing so the graph stays acyclic.
invariants: the stored reference graph is always acyclic
tradeoffs: Each write pays an O(V+E) reachability search

clarifyingQuestions: Does a redirect jump to the nearest server or the farthest?
What happens when no server lies on the diagonal?
Is the answer the final coordinate?
hints: Points on one diagonal share x-y (or x+y).
Group servers by diagonal key and sort by x.
Binary-search the neighbour on the correct side for each redirect.
invariants: each server appears once in each of its two diagonal lists
chooseWhen: Many redirects over a fixed fleet
tradeoffs: O(n log n) preprocessing; a per-redirect scan would be O(n)
hack2hire:6a330d046849fecc81440a2f.variantLabel: Inferred: nearest server along each diagonal

constraints: amounts are non-negative decimals with at most two fractional digits
clarifyingQuestions: What columns does an expense row have?
Does a rule describe what is allowed or what is forbidden?
In what order should violations be reported?
hints: A rule applies only when its conditional matches.
Compare money exactly, in integer cents.
Loop rules then expenses, recording [ruleId, expenseId] when the requirement fails.
invariants: amounts are compared as integer cents
tradeoffs: O(R*E) is simple; indexing by conditional value would help only with many rules

constraints: amounts are non-negative decimals with at most two fractional digits
clarifyingQuestions: What does a trip rule aggregate?
Are trips without matching expenses evaluated?
How are trip violations ordered?
hints: Trip rules apply to sums, not single expenses.
Accumulate applicable amounts per trip in first-appearance order.
Check each trip total against the requirement.
invariants: trip sums include only expenses passing the conditional
tradeoffs: An insertion-ordered map keeps output order without sorting

clarifyingQuestions: Is time passed into each call?
Does a retried task go to the front or the back?
Does fail() count as an attempt?
hints: Expire stale leases before handling any call.
Keep leases in a min-heap by deadline.
Stale heap entries can be skipped by checking the current holder sequence number.
invariants: a task is in at most one of ready, reserved, done, dead
attempts never exceed maxAttempts
tradeoffs: Lazy heap deletion trades memory for O(log n) updates

constraints: dependencies form a DAG, up to 40000 edges
clarifyingQuestions: Is time passed into each call?
Does a retried task go to the front or the back?
Does fail() count as an attempt?
What happens to dependents of a dead-lettered task?
hints: A task becomes ready when its last prerequisite completes.
Count missing prerequisites per task.
When a task dies, walk its dependents breadth-first and dead-letter them.
invariants: missing count = prerequisites not yet completed
dead tasks never become ready
tradeoffs: Cascading dead-letters makes failures visible immediately

clarifyingQuestions: What exactly must be answered: one check, a list of accessible entities, or both?
Is an unknown uuid an error or false?
Do teams nest?
hints: Access to a node means access to its whole subtree.
Number nodes by DFS entry time; a subtree is a contiguous interval.
For each user keep the outermost granted intervals and binary-search the query node.
invariants: subtree of v = entry times in [tin(v), tout(v)]
kept intervals per user are disjoint and sorted
chooseWhen: Many queries over a static tree
tradeoffs: Preprocessing is O(N log N); walking ancestors per query costs O(depth)

clarifyingQuestions: Is the input a digit string or separate numbers?
May numbers be concatenated?
Should all expressions be returned or just one?
hints: Different groupings can print the same string; count canonical forms instead.
A sum is a sequence of non-sum parts; a product is a sequence of non-product factors.
Memoise the forms of each operand interval with their values.
invariants: each rendering is produced exactly once
parentheses appear only around a sum used as a factor
chooseWhen: Small operand counts with an exhaustive answer
tradeoffs: Output can be exponential in k, so k stays small
hack2hire:67c76f386c89e288437c3031.variantLabel: Inferred: every minimally-parenthesised +/* expression hitting the target

clarifyingQuestions: Is an end time inclusive?
What is returned when no slot exists?
Does the action word ever mean free time?

Sort intervals by start and sweep.
The first gap of at least k free minutes gives the answer.

clarifyingQuestions: Should output ranges be strings or integers?
Are touching ranges merged?
hints: Free space lies between allocations.
Sort allocations by start.
Emit each gap between consecutive ranges and after the last one.
invariants: cursor is the first ID not yet accounted for

clarifyingQuestions: What does the follow-up add: a size filter, an allocation, or a bucket filter?
hints: Reuse the gap sweep.
Measure each gap as end-start+1.
Keep gaps at least minSize long.
invariants: returned gaps are maximal
chooseWhen: Allocating a block of a given size
tradeoffs: Same cost as level 1
hack2hire:6a7cd38bd713d873ca7ac6f0.variantLabel: Inferred level 2: free ranges of a minimum size

clarifyingQuestions: How are addresses delimited inside a line?
Are leading zeros allowed?
Lexicographic order of strings or of numeric octets?

constraints: up to 5000 undirected friendships, no duplicates
